promptHead: Athlete goal: 5K (Corrowmore Harvest 5K) on Sun Nov 15 2026, 10 weeks out, target run the whole way.

new.headline: Keep to three run days with a rest day between them, and make the run segments feel easier than they did last week. Next week steps up by about 6 minutes in total, which is enough progress at this stage.

flags.title: Effort too high
flags.detail: Your run segments felt 6 to 7 out of 10 and 27% of your running time was in zone 3. Slow down so it feels 4 to 5 out of 10, with heart rate under about 135.

flags.title: Calf tightness
flags.detail: Your calves were tight the day after each run and clear by the next morning. That is common for new runners. If it lasts longer, turns sharp or hurts on one side, cut back and see a physio.

flags.title: Rest days
flags.detail: Keep at least one full day between runs. Dog walks are fine on those days, so keep them relaxed and flat.

answers.question: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?
answers.answer:
No, don't run every day next week. Your fitness improves faster than your calves, tendons and joints adapt, and they need rest days to cope with each run. Your calves are already tight the day after each run, which tells me three run days is plenty for now.

Three runs with a rest day between, plus your dog walks, is the quickest safe route. The gain comes from lengthening the run pieces week by week, and ten weeks is enough time for that. Extra running now risks a niggle that costs you weeks, which sets you back more than a rest day does.

new.analysis:
Last week was a solid start. You ran all three planned mornings, covered 6.78 km in about an hour, and had no pain. The run-walk pattern worked, so there is no reason to change it, only to run it a little more gently.

Effort is the main thing to fix. Your run segments were at about 7:40/km and felt 6 to 7 out of 10, with heart rate touching zone 3. A new runner gets more from easy running because it lets you repeat the sessions and lengthen the run pieces later. If the run segments feel hard now, the longer ones will not be possible in a few weeks. Slow down until you could chat in short sentences, even if the pace drops.

The training phase says build, but you have only just started running. That means no hard sessions for now. Every run this week is easy, and speed work is not needed to run a 5K without walking. Time on your feet is what counts.

Your finish will probably take around 40 minutes of running. The job over the next ten weeks is to build up to that without a walk break. I will make the run pieces longer and the walks shorter a little at a time. Roughly every fourth week will be lighter so your body can catch up.

This week the total goes from about 64 to 70 minutes, an increase of roughly 10%. I have also added a short strength session. It targets your calves and hips, which take the load when you are new to running. Keep it light, and skip it if your calves still feel sore.
